about: The chapters of two TU Wien lecture notes, Kugi (2015), Automatisierung (WS 2015/16), and Kugi et al. (2015), Modellbildung (SS 2015), each chapter in a family that colours its cards, with the labs it teaches; then each lab's words and practice questions. Chapter numbers, titles (translated) and page ranges are those of the notes' tables of contents and page headers; equation numbers are the notes' own, checked against the PDFs' text on 1 Nov 2026. Practice answers are worked by hand; tests/unit/labs-data.test.js recomputes each with the core and fails if they disagree.

labs.title: Series resonant circuit
labs.idea: A circuit's state is what its energy stores hold: the capacitor's voltage and the coil's current. Two states, two first-order equations.
labs.lawTex: \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\begin{bmatrix} u_\mathrm{C} \\ i_\mathrm{L} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \frac{1}{C} \\ -\frac{1}{L} & -\frac{R}{L} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u_\mathrm{C} \\ i_\mathrm{L} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \frac{1}{L} \end{bmatrix} u \qquad y = R\, i_\mathrm{L}

practice.question: The series resonant circuit has R = 1 Ω, L = 1 H and C = 1 F, as in the notes' Figure 1.5. At what angular frequency ω do its states ring?

equations.eq: −u + uC + uL + y = 0,   iC − iL = 0,   iL − iR = 0
equations.tex: -u + u_\mathrm{C} + u_\mathrm{L} + y = 0, \qquad i_\mathrm{C} - i_\mathrm{L} = 0, \qquad i_\mathrm{L} - i_\mathrm{R} = 0

equations.eq: C duC/dt = iC,   L diL/dt = uL,   R iR = y
equations.tex: C \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} u_\mathrm{C} = i_\mathrm{C}, \qquad L \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} i_\mathrm{L} = u_\mathrm{L}, \qquad R\, i_\mathrm{R} = y

equations.note: decay rate τ and ringing frequency of the free response (1.10)

labs.title: DC motor
labs.idea: The armature voltage sets the motor's speed and the load sets its current: at rest the motor's torque balances the load.
labs.law: LA diA/dt = uA − RA iA − K ω    J dω/dt = K iA − m g r
labs.lawTex: L_\mathrm{A} \frac{\mathrm{d}i_\mathrm{A}}{\mathrm{d}t} = u_\mathrm{A} - R_\mathrm{A} i_\mathrm{A} - K\omega \qquad J \frac{\mathrm{d}\omega}{\mathrm{d}t} = K i_\mathrm{A} - mgr

practice.question: A DC motor with constant excitation has K = kΨF = 0.1 V·s and RA = 1 Ω. It is fed with uA = 12 V and holds a load torque m g r = 0.05 N·m. What speed ω does it settle at?
practice.solution: At rest dω/dt = 0 gives K iA = m g r, so iA = 0.05/0.1 = 0.5 A. Then diA/dt = 0 gives uA = RA iA + K ω, so ω = (12 − 1·0.5)/0.1 = 115 rad/s.

equations.eq: diA/dt = (uA − RA iA − k ψF(iF) ω)/LA
dω/dt = (k ψF(iF) iA − m g r)/(ΘG + ΘT + m r²)
equations.note: speed of the drum with the load on its cable

equations.eq: iA,R = m g r/K,   ωR = (uA − RA iA,R)/K
equations.note: rest state with K = k ψF constant (derived from (1.25a), (1.25d))

labs.title: Two tanks and linearisation
labs.idea: Near a rest state (Ruhelage) a nonlinear system behaves like its linearisation; the further it strays, the worse the match.
labs.law: A dh1/dt = q − a√(2g h1)    A dh2/dt = a√(2g h1) − a√(2g h2)    Δẋ = (∂f/∂x) Δx + (∂f/∂u) Δu
labs.lawTex: A \frac{\mathrm{d}h_1}{\mathrm{d}t} = q - a\sqrt{2g h_1} \qquad A \frac{\mathrm{d}h_2}{\mathrm{d}t} = a\sqrt{2g h_1} - a\sqrt{2g h_2} \qquad \Delta\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \Delta\mathbf{x} + \frac{\partial \mathbf{f}}{\partial \mathbf{u}} \Delta\mathbf{u}

practice.question: Both tanks of the two-tank system have outlets of a = 5·10⁻⁵ m² (0.5 cm²). The steady inflow is qR = 10⁻⁴ m³/s and g = 9.81 m/s². At what level h1,R = h2,R do the tanks rest?
practice.solution: At rest dh1/dt = 0, so a√(2g h1,R) = qR and h1,R = qR²/(2g a²) = 10⁻⁸/(2·9.81·2.5·10⁻⁹) = 0.204 m. The second tank passes the same flow, so h2,R = h1,R.

equations.eq: A dh1/dt = q − q1,   A dh2/dt = q1 − q2
equations.tex: A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} h_1 = q - q_1, \qquad A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} h_2 = q_1 - q_2
q_1 = a\sqrt{2g h_1}, \qquad q_2 = a\sqrt{2g h_2}

equations.eq: A dh1/dt = −a√(2g h1) + q,   A dh2/dt = a√(2g)(√h1 − √h2)
equations.tex: A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} h_1 = -a\sqrt{2g}\sqrt{h_1} + q, \qquad A \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} h_2 = a\sqrt{2g}\big(\sqrt{h_1} - \sqrt{h_2}\big)

equations.eq: Δẋ = A Δx + B Δu,   Δy = C Δx + D Δu
A = ∂f/∂x,   B = ∂f/∂u,   C = ∂h/∂x,   D = ∂h/∂u   at (xR, uR)

equations.tex: h_{1,R} = h_{2,R} = \frac{q_R^2}{2 g a^2}, \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\begin{bmatrix} \Delta h_1 \\ \Delta h_2 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{a^2 g}{A q_R} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \Delta h_1 \\ \Delta h_2 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{A} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \Delta q

labs.title: Solution behaviour of ẋ = Ax
labs.idea: A linear system without input, ẋ = Ax, rests at x = 0. Start it anywhere and the state x = (x1, x2) traces a path, its trajectory; drawn for many starts, the paths form the phase portrait. The two eigenvalues of A alone decide its shape. Real ones of the same sign give a node: the paths run in, or out, without turning. Real ones of opposite sign give a saddle: in along one direction, out along the other. Complex ones α ± jβ make the paths turn: a focus spirals in when α < 0 and out when α > 0, and a centre (α = 0) circles forever. Negative real parts bring every start home.
labs.law: x(t) = Φ(t) x0 = exp(At) x0

practice.question: Example 3.3 of the notes has A = [[1.4, −1.2], [−1.2, −0.4]]. What is its larger eigenvalue, the one trajectories leave along?
practice.solution: det(λE − A) = λ² − (trace A)λ + det A = λ² − 1.0λ − 2 = (λ − 2)(λ + 1). So λ1 = −1 and λ2 = 2: a saddle, unstable.

equations.note: transition matrix of a time-invariant system

equations.eq: t^k1 e^(λt),   t^k2 e^(αt) cos(βt),   t^k3 e^(αt) sin(βt)
equations.tex: t^{k_1} \mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}, \qquad t^{k_2} \mathrm{e}^{\alpha t} \cos(\beta t), \qquad t^{k_3} \mathrm{e}^{\alpha t} \sin(\beta t)
equations.note: the functions every solution is built from (Satz 3.3); λ real, α ± Iβ complex eigenvalues

equations.eq: lim x(t) = lim Φ(t) x0 = 0  ⇔  all Re λ < 0

equations.note: a start on an eigenvector stays on it

labs.title: Nyquist locus
labs.idea: The frequency response G(jω) is a point in the complex plane for each ω; together they draw a curve, the Nyquist locus (Ortskurve).
labs.law: ω ↦ (Re G(Iω), Im G(Iω))

practice.question: The Nyquist locus of G(s) = (10s² + 15s + 10)/(s² + s + 3), the notes' (3.114), crosses the real axis at ω0 > 0. What is ω0?
practice.solution: G(jω) = (10 − 10ω² + j15ω)/(3 − ω² + jω). Multiply by the conjugate of the denominator: the imaginary part of the numerator is 15ω(3 − ω²) − ω(10 − 10ω²) = ω(35 − 5ω²). It vanishes at ω0² = 7, so ω0 = √7 = 2.65 rad/s (Aufgabe 3.26).

equations.eq: y(t) = A0 |G(Iω0)| sin(ω0 t + arg G(Iω0))
equations.note: steady response to a sine input

labs.title: Bode diagram
labs.idea: On logarithmic axes the parts of a transfer function add: each factor contributes straight asymptotes, and the sum is the whole.
labs.law: |G(Iω)|dB = Σ |Gi(Iω)|dB    arg G(Iω) = Σ arg Gi(Iω)

practice.question: Take the notes' example in normalised form, G(s) = 10(1 − s/10)/(s(1 + 2·½·s/0.1 + s²/0.1²)). What does the asymptotic magnitude read at ω = 1 rad/s?
practice.solution: Gain: 20 log 10 = 20 dB. Integrator: −20 log 1 = 0 dB. Pole pair at 0.1 rad/s: one decade past its corner, −40 dB. Zero at 10 rad/s: not reached, 0 dB. Sum: −20 dB.

practice.question: Same G(s): what does the asymptote read at ω = 0.01 rad/s, below every corner?
practice.solution: Only the gain and the integrator count: 20 log 10 − 20 log 0.01 = 20 + 40 = 60 dB.

equations.note: magnitudes of a series connection add

equations.eq: G(s) = V z(s)/(s^r n(s)), with factors 1 + s/ωk and 1 + 2ξk s/ωk + s²/ωk²
|1 + Iω/ωk|dB ≈ 0 for ω ≪ ωk, 20 log(ω/ωk) for ω ≫ ωk
|1 − (ω/ωk)² + I2ξk ω/ωk|dB ≈ 0 for ω ≪ ωk, 40 log(ω/ωk) for ω ≫ ωk

labs.title: First-order lag
labs.idea: A first-order lag (P-T1 element) follows a step along an exponential: V says where it ends, T how fast it gets there.

practice.question: For the notes' example G(s) = 10/(1 + s/2), so V = 10 and T = 0.5 s, what is the step response at t = 0.5 s?
practice.solution: h(T) = V(1 − e⁻¹) = 10 · 0.632 = 6.32, 63 % of the final value.

practice.question: Same element: what is the slope of the step response at t = 0?
practice.solution: dh/dt = (V/T) e^(−t/T), which at t = 0 is V/T = 10/0.5 = 20 1/s (Aufgabe 3.33).

labs.title: Second-order lag
labs.idea: The damping of a second-order lag (P-T2 element) decides how far it overshoots and how long it rings; the time constant only stretches time.

practice.question: A P-T2 element has T = 0.1 s and ξ = 0.5. What is the imaginary part of its upper pole, the frequency it rings at?
With V = 5 and ξ = 0.5, what is the peak value of the step response?
practice.solution: The first maximum of (3.138) is where √(1 − ξ²) t/T = π. There the bracket gives h = V(1 + e^(−πξ/√(1 − ξ²))) = 5(1 + e^(−1.814)) = 5 · 1.163 = 5.82.

equations.note: gain V, time constant T, damping 0 ≤ ξ < 1

equations.eq: g(t) = V/(T√(1 − ξ²)) e^(−ξt/T) sin(√(1 − ξ²) t/T) σ(t)

labs.title: Controller elements
labs.idea: P answers now, I remembers the past and D looks ahead: the controller elements combine them, each with its own step response and Bode diagram.
labs.law: G(s) = VP (1 + TI s)(1 + TD s)/(s(1 + TR s))
labs.lawTex: G(s) = V_\mathrm{P} \frac{(1 + T_\mathrm{I} s)(1 + T_\mathrm{D} s)}{s(1 + T_\mathrm{R} s)}

practice.question: A lead element G(s) = V(1 + sT)/(1 + αsT) has T = 1 s and α = 0.1, as in Aufgabe 3.42. What is its largest phase lift φmax?
practice.solution: The phase peaks at ωmax = 1/(T√α) = 3.16 rad/s, where φmax = arctan(1/√α) − arctan(√α) = arctan(3.162) − arctan(0.316) = 72.5° − 17.5° = 54.9°.

practice.question: A PI element has VI = 2 1/s and TI = 0.5 s. What is its step response at t = 1 s?
practice.solution: h(t) = VI t + VI TI (Aufgabe 3.37) = 2 · 1 + 2 · 0.5 = 3.

equations.eq: G(s) = VI(1 + sTI)/s = VI/s + VI TI

equations.note: largest phase lift of the lead element

equations.eq: G(s) = VP(1 + TI s)(1 + TD s)/(s(1 + TR s))
equations.tex: G(s) = V_\mathrm{P} \frac{(1 + T_\mathrm{I} s)(1 + T_\mathrm{D} s)}{s(1 + T_\mathrm{R} s)}

labs.title: Dead time
labs.idea: A dead time (Totzeit) passes the input on unchanged but late, which costs phase in proportion to the frequency.
labs.law: y(t) = u(t − Tt)    G(s) = e^(−sTt)

practice.question: A conveyor gives a dead time Tt = 0.2 s. By what phase does its output lag a sine input of ω = 5 rad/s?
practice.solution: G(jω) = e^(−jωTt) has magnitude 1 and phase −ωTt = −5 · 0.2 = −1 rad = −57.3°.

equations.note: the input shifted by the dead time
transfer function, by the shift theorem

labs.title: Pole-zero diagram
labs.idea: Where the poles sit tells how a system responds: left of the imaginary axis it is BIBO stable, and a pole pair's angle and distance give its damping and time constant.
labs.law: ξ = −α/√(α² + β²)    T = 1/√(α² + β²)

practice.question: The notes' example (3.163) has the pole pair −2 ± j1.5. What damping ξ does it have?
And what time constant T?
practice.solution: T = 1/√(σ² + ω²) = 1/2.5 = 0.4 s: the pair lies on the half circle of radius 2.5.

equations.eq: n(s) = (s − α − Iβ)(s − α + Iβ) = 1/T² + 2ξ s/T + s²
equations.note: a pole pair as a P-T2 denominator
damping: constant on a ray through the origin
time constant: constant on a circle about the origin

equations.eq: Re(si) = αi < 0 for every pole si

labs.title: Control loop with one degree of freedom
labs.idea: One controller sets both how the output follows the reference and how much of a disturbance is left; an integrator in the loop removes the steady-state error.
labs.law: Tr,y = RG/(1 + RG)    Td,y = S = 1/(1 + RG)    Tr,y + Td,y = 1
labs.lawTex: T_{r,y} = \frac{RG}{1 + RG} \qquad T_{d,y} = S = \frac{1}{1 + RG} \qquad T_{r,y} + T_{d,y} = 1

practice.question: The open loop is L(s) = 8/(1 + s)², a plant 2/(1 + s)² under a P controller with gain 4. What steady-state error e∞ does a unit reference step leave?
practice.solution: L has no pole at s = 0 (ρ = 0) and gain V = 8, so by (5.10) e∞ = 1/(1 + V) = 1/9 = 0.111.

practice.question: With a PI controller the open loop becomes L(s) = 2/(s(1 + s)). What steady-state error e∞ does a unit ramp r(t) = t leave?
practice.solution: One pole at s = 0 (ρ = 1) and V = 2, so by (5.10) e∞ = 1/V = 0.5 for the ramp; a step would leave none.

equations.eq: Tr,y = R G/(1 + R G),   Td,y = Gd/(1 + R G),   Tn,y = −R G/(1 + R G)
equations.tex: T_{r,y} = \frac{RG}{1 + RG}, \qquad T_{d,y} = \frac{G_d}{1 + RG}, \qquad T_{n,y} = \frac{-RG}{1 + RG}
equations.note: reference, disturbance and noise to the output

equations.eq: Tr,y = L/(1 + L),   Td,y = 1/(1 + L),   L = R G
equations.tex: T_{r,y} = \frac{L}{1 + L}, \qquad T_{d,y} = \frac{1}{1 + L}, \qquad L = RG
equations.note: with Gd = 1, the disturbance acting at the output
the input the controller asks for
so T = 1 − S is the complementary sensitivity

equations.eq: step: e∞ = 1/(1 + V) for ρ = 0, 0 for ρ = 1;   ramp: e∞ = ∞ for ρ = 0, 1/V for ρ = 1
equations.tex: r = \sigma(t)\!: \; e_\infty = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{1 + V} & \rho = 0 \\ 0 & \rho = 1 \end{cases} \qquad r = t\!: \; e_\infty = \begin{cases} \infty & \rho = 0 \\ \frac{1}{V} & \rho = 1 \end{cases}

labs.title: Routh–Hurwitz test
labs.idea: Whether every root of a polynomial lies in the left half plane can be read from its coefficients alone, without computing a root.

practice.question: The loop of Beispiel 4.4 has R(s) = K/s and G(s) = 9/(s² + 3s + 9). Up to what gain K is the closed loop stable?
practice.solution: The closed loop's denominator is s³ + 3s² + 9s + 9K (4.34). The Routh array has the pivot column 1, 3, (3·9 − 9K)/3 = 9 − 3K, 9K (4.35). All positive needs 9 − 3K > 0 and 9K > 0, so 0 < K < 3 (4.36).

equations.eq: n(s) = a_n sⁿ + … + a_1 s + a_0: all a_j ≠ 0 with one sign
equations.tex: n(s) = a_n s^n + \dots + a_1 s + a_0\!: \quad \text{all } a_j \ne 0 \text{ with the same sign}
equations.note: necessary for a Hurwitz polynomial, also sufficient for n = 2 (Satz 4.2)
the Routh array; its first column is the pivot column
the entries; Hurwitz exactly when the pivot column has no zero and one sign (Satz 4.3)
the stable range of the gain

labs.title: Nyquist criterion
labs.idea: The locus of the open loop L(jω) and the point −1 decide whether the closed loop is stable; the phase margin says how far it is from the edge.
labs.law: Δarg(1 + L(Iω)) = (max(grad zL, grad nL) − N₋(nL) + N₊(nL))·π    Φ = arg L(IωC) + π

practice.question: The open loop is L(s) = K/(s(s + 1)²) with K = 0.5 (Aufgabe 4.12). By what factor may the gain grow before the closed loop becomes unstable?
practice.solution: arg L(jω) = −90° − 2·arctan ω = −180° at ω = 1 rad/s. There |L| = 0.5/(1·(1 + 1)) = 0.25, so the locus crosses the real axis at −0.25 and K may grow by 1/0.25 = 4, to K = 2.

practice.question: For the same loop with K = 0.5, what is the phase margin Φ?

equations.eq: Δarg(1 + L(Iω)) = (max(grad zL, grad nL) − N₋(nL) + N₊(nL))·π
equations.note: Nyquist criterion (Satz 4.5): stable exactly when this holds
the form for the Bode version (Satz 4.6)
not defined in the notes; the usual reading of the same locus

labs.title: PI design by loop shaping
labs.idea: Rise time and overshoot of the closed loop translate into a crossover frequency and a phase margin of the open loop, which a PI controller can set.

practice.question: For the plant G(s) = 5/(1 + 1.414s + s²) the targets are ωC = 0.5 rad/s and Φ = 60°, and arg L1(jωC) = −133.3° for L1 = G/s. What time constant TI must the PI controller's zero have?
practice.solution: The loop needs arg L(jωC) = Φ − 180° = −120°, so the zero must add 13.3°: arctan(ωC·TI) = 13.3° (5.16), TI = tan 13.3°/0.5 = 0.47 s.

practice.question: With TI = 0.47 s, what gain VI puts the crossover at ωC = 0.5 rad/s?

equations.eq: Tr,y = R G/(1 + R G) = L/(1 + L)
equations.note: the closed loop to be shaped
rise time from the crossover frequency (Durchtrittsfrequenz)
the plant; targets tr = 3 s, ü = 10 %, e∞ = 0

equations.eq: arg(1 + IωC TI) = arctan(ωC·TI) = Φ − 180° − arg L1(IωC)
equations.note: the zero lifts the phase; in the notes' case by 13.3°

labs.title: Sampled systems and the sample time
labs.idea: Behind a zero-order hold a continuous plant becomes a difference equation whose poles are e^{sTa}; a few samples per rise time are enough.
labs.law: x_{k+1} = Φx_k + Γu_k,  Φ = exp(ATa),  Γ = ∫₀^Ta exp(Aτ) dτ b    z = e^{sTa}    tr/Ta ≈ 4 to 10

practice.question: A P-T2 plant has T2 = 1 s and damping ξ = 0.5. What is its rise time tr?
practice.solution: arccos 0.5 = π/3 = 1.047 and tan(π/3) = 1.732, so by (6.61) tr = 1·exp(1.047/1.732) = e^0.605 = 1.83 s. By (6.62) Ta should lie between 0.18 s and 0.46 s.

practice.question: A continuous plant has a pole at s = −2 1/s. Where does the sampled system's pole lie for Ta = 0.1 s?
practice.solution: By Satz 6.3 the pole moves to z = e^{sTa} = e^{−0.2} = 0.819, inside the unit circle as a stable pole must.

equations.eq: x_{k+1} = Φx_k + Γu_k,   y_k = Cx_k + Du_k
Φ = exp(ATa),   Γ = ∫₀^Ta exp(Aτ) dτ B
s_j pole of G(s)   ⇒   e^{s_j Ta} pole of G(z)
equations.tex: s_j \text{ pole of } G(s) \;\Rightarrow\; \mathrm{e}^{s_j T_\mathrm{a}} \text{ pole of } G(z)
equations.note: the left half plane maps into the unit circle
rule of thumb for the sample time (Abtastzeit)

labs.title: Tustin transformation and frequency warping
labs.idea: Substituting q = (2/Ta)(z − 1)/(z + 1) for s keeps a controller's shape but bends its frequency axis: what sat at Ω now sits at a lower ω.

practice.question: With Ta = 0.1 s, which transformed frequency Ω belongs to ω = 10 rad/s?
A filter designed with its resonance at 10 rad/s is discretised by Tustin with Ta = 0.1 s. At what real frequency ω does the discrete filter peak?
practice.solution: The peak lies where Ω = 10: tan(ωTa/2) = 10·0.1/2 = 0.5, so ω = 20·arctan 0.5 = 20·0.4636 = 9.27 rad/s (6.89 solved for ω).

equations.note: the unit circle onto the imaginary axis
transformed frequency; 0 ≤ ω < π/Ta fills 0 ≤ Ω < ∞
its inverse, the bilinear transformation after Tustin

labs.title: Reachability
labs.idea: An input can steer a linear system from rest to any state exactly when the reachability matrix has full rank.
labs.law: R(A, b) = [b, Ab, …, A^{n−1}b],  rank n    u(t) = bᵀe^{Aᵀ(T−t)}G⁻¹x(T)

practice.question: A = diag(−1, −3) and b = [1, 1]. What is the determinant of the reachability matrix R(A, b)?
For the same system, what is the off-diagonal entry of the Gramian G for T → ∞?
practice.solution: A is a Hurwitz matrix, so G solves AG + GAᵀ + bbᵀ = 0 (7.21). The off-diagonal entry gives −G12 − 3G12 + 1 = 0, so G12 = 1/4 = 0.25.

equations.note: reachability matrix (Erreichbarkeitsmatrix); reachable exactly when rank n (Satz 7.1)

equations.eq: G = ∫₀ᵀ e^{Aτ} B Bᵀ e^{Aᵀτ} dτ
equations.note: Gramian (Gramsche Matrix), regular for every T > 0 when reachable

equations.eq: A G∞ + G∞ Aᵀ + B Bᵀ = 0
equations.note: the Gramian for T → ∞ when A is a Hurwitz matrix

labs.title: State controller by pole placement
labs.idea: Feeding back the whole state places the closed loop's poles anywhere, provided the system is reachable; with all poles at zero it settles in n steps.
labs.law: u_k = kᵀx_k + g r_k    kᵀ = −v1ᵀ p_g,soll(Φ),  v1ᵀ = e_nᵀ R(Φ, Γ)⁻¹

practice.question: For x_{k+1} = [[1, 1], [0, 1]]x_k + [0, 1]u_k a dead-beat controller is wanted (Aufgabe 8.5). What is the second entry k2 of kᵀ?
With that controller and y_k = x_{1,k}, what prefilter g gives y_k → r?
practice.solution: Φ + Γkᵀ = [[1, 1], [−1, −1]], so E − Φ − Γkᵀ = [[0, −1], [1, 2]] with inverse [[2, 1], [−1, 0]]. Times Γ gives [1, 0], and cᵀ of that is 1, so g = 1/1 = 1 (8.39).

equations.eq: x_{k+1} = Φx_k + Γu_k,   y_k = cᵀx_k + du_k
e_nᵀ = v1ᵀ[Γ, ΦΓ, …, Φ^{n−1}Γ],   kᵀ = −v1ᵀ p_g,soll(Φ)
p_g,soll(z) = zⁿ   ⇒   x_k = Φ_gᵏ x_0 = 0 for k ≥ n

labs.title: Luenberger observer and the separation principle
labs.idea: A model of the plant corrected by the measured output estimates the full state; controller and observer can be designed apart, their poles simply add up.
labs.law: x̂_{k+1} = Φx̂_k + Γu_k + k̂(ŷ_k − y_k)    e_{k+1} = (Φ + k̂cᵀ)e_k    p_ges = p_g,soll · p̂_g,soll

practice.question: For x_{k+1} = [[2, 1], [0, 10]]x_k + [0, 1]u_k with y_k = x_{1,k} a dead-beat observer is wanted (Aufgabe 8.9). What is the second entry of k̂?
practice.solution: Φ + k̂cᵀ = [[2 + k̂1, 1], [k̂2, 10]] must have trace 0 and determinant 0 (8.66): k̂1 = −12, then 10(2 + k̂1) − k̂2 = −100 − k̂2 = 0 gives k̂2 = −100, as Aufgabe 8.9 states.

equations.eq: x̂_{k+1} = Φx̂_k + Γu_k + k̂(ŷ_k − y_k),   ŷ_k = cᵀx̂_k + du_k
k̂ = −p̂_g,soll(Φ) v̂1,   e_n = O(cᵀ, Φ) v̂1
equations.note: Ackermann's formula for the observer (Satz 8.5), needs complete observability

equations.eq: Φᵀ for Φ,   c for Γ,   k̂ for k

equations.note: the controller fed by the estimate

equations.eq: p_ges(z) = det(zE − Φ − Γkᵀ)·det(zE − Φ − k̂cᵀ)

labs.title: Point kinematics
labs.idea: Velocity is the integral of acceleration and position the integral of velocity, so an acceleration profile fixes where a mass stops.
labs.law: v(t) = v(t0) + ∫ a dτ    x(t) = x(t0) + ∫ v dτ
labs.lawTex: v(t) = v(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t} a(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau \qquad x(t) = x(t_0) + \int_{t_0}^{t} v(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau
labs.lecture: Kugi et al. (2015), section 2.1, Example 2.1 (pp. 8–9); eq. (2.5)–(2.11)

practice.question: As in Example 2.1, a mass starts at rest at x = 0 at t0 = 0, accelerates with amax = 2 m/s² until t1 = 1 s, coasts until t2 = 3 s, then brakes so that it stops at xsoll = 8 m. What braking acceleration amin is needed?
practice.solution: By (2.11) with t0 = 0: amin = −amax² t1² / (amax t1 (t1 − 2 t2) + 2 xsoll) = −4 / (2 · (1 − 6) + 16) = −4/6 = −0.667 m/s². Check: 1 m while speeding up, 4 m coasting at 2 m/s, and v²/(2|amin|) = 3 m braking, 8 m in all.

equations.eq: v1(t) = v0 + amax (t − t0),   x1(t) = x0 + v0 (t − t0) + ½ amax (t − t0)²
equations.tex: v_1(t) = v_0 + a_\mathrm{max}(t - t_0), \qquad x_1(t) = x_0 + v_0(t - t_0) + \frac{1}{2} a_\mathrm{max}(t - t_0)^2
equations.note: speeding up; the notes take v0 = x0 = 0, the lab keeps them general

equations.eq: v2(t) = amax (t1 − t0),   x2(t) = ½ amax (t1 − t0)² + amax (t1 − t0)(t − t1)
equations.tex: v_2(t) = a_\mathrm{max}(t_1 - t_0), \qquad x_2(t) = \frac{1}{2} a_\mathrm{max}(t_1 - t_0)^2 + a_\mathrm{max}(t_1 - t_0)(t - t_1)

equations.eq: amin = −amax² (t1 − t0)² / (amax (t1 − t0)(t1 + t0 − 2 t2) + 2 xsoll)
equations.note: the braking that stops at xsoll

labs.title: Conservation of momentum
labs.idea: When two masses meet, the forces between them cancel, so their total momentum is the same before and after.
labs.law: (mi + mj) d²rS/dt² = fi + fj

practice.question: A 2 kg block moving at 3 m/s runs into a 1 kg block at rest, and they stick together (plastic, e = 0). How fast does the 2 kg block move afterwards?
practice.solution: No outside force acts along the track, so momentum is kept, (2.71): 2 · 3 + 1 · 0 = (2 + 1) u, so u = 2 m/s.

practice.question: In the same plastic collision, how much kinetic energy is lost?
practice.solution: By (2.81), before: ½ · 2 · 3² = 9 J; after: ½ · 3 · 2² = 6 J; lost: 3 J, to heat and deformation.

equations.note: conservation of momentum (Impulserhaltungssatz) for a point mass

equations.eq: mi dvi/dt = fi + fij,   mj dvj/dt = fj + fji,   fij = −fji
equations.note: two masses with forces between them
the internal forces cancel; the centre of mass moves as one mass
velocities after a short impact with coefficient of restitution e (not in the notes)

labs.title: Kinetic and potential energy
labs.idea: A mass on a spring trades kinetic for potential energy and back, and with no friction their sum stays constant.
labs.law: T + V = ½ m v² + ½ c (s − s0)² = const
labs.lawTex: T + V = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 + \frac{1}{2} c (s - s_0)^2 = \text{const}

practice.question: A 0.5 kg mass on a spring of rate c = 200 N/m is pulled 0.1 m from the spring's free length and let go. How fast is it moving when it passes the free length?
practice.solution: By (2.92) the spring holds ½ · 200 · 0.1² = 1 J. At s = s0 all of it is kinetic, (2.81): ½ · 0.5 · v² = 1 J, so v = 2 m/s.

equations.eq: V(s) = ∫ fF(s̃) ds̃ from s0 to s

labs.title: Friction
labs.idea: Friction turns motion into heat: dry (Coulomb) friction stops a sliding block at a steady rate, viscous friction fades it gradually.
labs.law: m ẍ = fe − µC m g sign(ẋ) − µV ẋ

practice.question: A block slides on a floor at 2 m/s with only Coulomb friction, µC = 0.4, and no push. With g = 9.81 m/s², how far does it slide before it stops?
practice.solution: By (2.101) with fe = 0 the block slows at µC g = 3.924 m/s², a constant. It stops after v0²/(2 µC g) = 4 / 7.848 = 0.510 m.

equations.eq: m ẍ = fe − µC m g sign(ẋ)
sticking: |fe| ≤ fH and ẋ = 0 ⇒ ẋ = 0; sliding otherwise
equations.tex: \lvert f_e \rvert \le f_H \text{ and } \dot{x} = 0\!: \; \dot{x} = 0 \qquad \text{otherwise}\!: \; m\dot{v} = f_e - \mu_C m g \operatorname{sign}(v)

equations.note: viscous friction; Δv is the relative speed

labs.title: Spring-mass-damper system
labs.idea: A mass on a spring and damper rings at its natural frequency, dies away through the damper, and answers a shaking force most strongly near that frequency.
labs.law: M q̈ + D q̇ + C q = B fe

practice.question: A 2 kg mass hangs on a spring of rate c = 800 N/m. What is its natural frequency ω0 = √(c/m)?
practice.solution: With one mass, (2.121) reads m q̈ + d q̇ + c q = f; undamped and free it oscillates as sin(ω0 t) with ω0 = √(c/m) = √400 = 20 rad/s.

practice.question: The same mass has a damper of d = 16 N s/m. What is the damping ratio ζ = d / (2√(cm))?
practice.solution: Dividing (2.121) by m gives q̈ + 2ζω0 q̇ + ω0² q = f/m with ζ = d / (2√(cm)) = 16 / (2 · 40) = 0.2.

equations.eq: M q̈ + D q̇ + C q = k + b fL
M q̈ + D q̇ + C q = B fe
equations.note: any linear spring-mass-damper system, about its rest position

equations.eq: T = ½ q̇ᵀ M q̇,   V = ½ qᵀ C q
dE/dt = −q̇ᵀ D q̇ + q̇ᵀ B fe
equations.note: the damper dissipates, the force supplies
one mass: natural frequency, damping ratio, steady amplitude

labs.title: Conservation of angular momentum
labs.idea: Under a central force the angular momentum is constant, so the line to the centre sweeps equal areas in equal times.

practice.question: A 0.5 kg puck circles a pin on a spring with angular momentum l = 0.3 kg m²/s about the pin. What area does the line from the pin sweep each second?
practice.solution: By (2.136), l(0) = 2 m dA(0)/dt, so dA/dt = l / (2m) = 0.3 / 1 = 0.3 m²/s, the same at every point of the path.

equations.eq: l(0) = r × p = r × m v
dA(0)/dt = ½ r × v,   l(0) = 2 m dA(0)/dt

labs.title: Euler–Lagrange equations
labs.idea: From the kinetic and potential energy alone, the Lagrangian gives the equations of motion of a ball rolling on a turning beam.
labs.law: d/dt ∂L/∂q̇j − ∂L/∂qj = fnp,j    L = T − V
labs.lawTex: \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_j} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_j} = f_{np,j} \qquad L = T - V

practice.question: A 0.1 kg ball rests on the beam of Example 2.20 at r = 0.2 m from the pivot, with the beam level. With g = 9.81 m/s², what torque on the beam holds it there?
practice.solution: Set all speeds and accelerations to zero with φ1 = 0 in (2.214): the first equation holds for any r, the second leaves τe(0) = g mK r = 9.81 · 0.1 · 0.2 = 0.196 N m.

equations.tex: \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} \frac{\partial}{\partial \dot{q}_j} L - \frac{\partial}{\partial q_j} L = f_{np,j}, \qquad L = T - V

equations.eq: Tt,K = ½ mK (r² φ̇1² + (ṙ − rK φ̇1)²)
θK,zz = 2/5 mK rK²,   Tr,K = ½ θK,zz (φ̇1 − ṙ/rK)²
Tr,B = ½ θB,zz φ̇1²,   V = mK g (r sin φ1 + rK cos φ1) − mK g rK
equations.tex: T_{r,B} = \frac{1}{2} \theta_{B,zz} \dot{\varphi}_1^2, \qquad V = m_K g \big(r \sin(\varphi_1) + r_K \cos(\varphi_1)\big) - m_K g r_K

equations.eq: (mK + θK,zz/rK²) r̈ − (θK,zz/rK + mK rK) φ̈1 − mK r φ̇1² + mK g sin φ1 = 0
equations.tex: \Big(m_K + \frac{\theta_{K,zz}}{r_K^2}\Big) \ddot{r} - \Big(\frac{\theta_{K,zz}}{r_K} + m_K r_K\Big) \ddot{\varphi}_1 - m_K r \dot{\varphi}_1^2 + m_K g \sin(\varphi_1) = 0

equations.eq: −(mK rK + θK,zz/rK) r̈ + (θK,zz + θB,zz + mK (r² + rK²)) φ̈1 + 2 mK r ṙ φ̇1 + mK g (r cos φ1 − rK sin φ1) = τe(0)
equations.tex: -\Big(m_K r_K + \frac{\theta_{K,zz}}{r_K}\Big) \ddot{r} + \Big(\theta_{K,zz} + \theta_{B,zz} + m_K\big(r^2 + r_K^2\big)\Big) \ddot{\varphi}_1 + 2 m_K r \dot{r} \dot{\varphi}_1 + m_K g \big(r \cos(\varphi_1) - r_K \sin(\varphi_1)\big) = \tau_e^{(0)}

labs.title: Heat radiation
labs.idea: Every surface radiates in proportion to T⁴; near room temperature that is about as much as gentle convection, and far more when hot.
labs.law: q′ = πD(α(T2 − T∞) + ε2σ(T2⁴ − T∞⁴))    Eb = σT⁴

practice.question: The vacuum-jacketed tube reactor of Beispiel 3.1: outer tube D = 100 mm, ε2 = 0.8, α = 10 W/(m²K), air and surroundings at T∞ = 20 °C. Its surface must stay at or below T2,max = 45 °C. What is the largest heat flow per metre q′ it may give off?

equations.note: Stefan–Boltzmann law for a black body
radiosity of a grey, opaque surface (net-radiation method)
net flux between concentric tubes; (3.63) divided by ε1ε2
loss of the outer tube by convection and radiation
inner tube temperature at full load
linearised radiation coefficient, so that εσ(T2⁴ − T∞⁴) = αrad(T2 − T∞)

labs.title: Plane wall
labs.idea: Through a layered wall the same heat flux crosses every layer, so the thermal resistances add like resistors in series.
labs.law: q = k(T∞,0 − T∞,L)    1/k = 1/α0 + Σ Li/λi + 1/αL

practice.question: Double glazing as in Beispiel 3.2: two panes of glass 4 mm thick (λG = 1 W/(m K)) with a 12 mm gap of still air (λL = 0.025 W/(m K)); αI = 8 W/(m²K) inside, αA = 20 W/(m²K) outside. What is its heat transfer coefficient kD?
For the same window, how many times larger is the heat transfer coefficient kE of a single pane of 4 mm glass, kE/kD?

equations.note: one layer, constant conductivity, surface temperatures given
the same flux through every layer and film

labs.title: Insulated pipe
labs.idea: Insulating a thin pipe also enlarges its surface, so up to a critical radius more insulation loses more heat.
labs.law: q′ = 2π(TF − T∞) / (1/(r0α0) + Σ ln(ri/ri−1)/λi + 1/(rNαN))    rc = λ/α

practice.question: A wire of radius 2 mm is held at 60 °C and sheathed in PVC (λ = 0.2 W/(m K)) to an outer radius of 10 mm; air at 20 °C, α = 10 W/(m²K). What heat flow per metre q′ leaves it?
practice.solution: With the inner surface at TF the term 1/(r0α0) vanishes: q′ = 2π × 40 K / (ln(10/2)/0.2 + 1/(0.01 × 10)) = 251.3 / (8.05 + 10) W/m = 13.9 W/m.

practice.question: For the same sheath, at what outer radius rc is the heat loss largest?
practice.solution: Only ln(rN/r0)/λ + 1/(rNα) in (3.93) depends on rN; its derivative 1/(λrN) − 1/(αrN²) is zero at rN = λ/α = 0.2/10 m = 20 mm.

equations.note: stationary conduction in layer i, no sources

labs.title: Cooling fins
labs.idea: A fin enlarges the surface, but it cools along its length, so each extra length adds less: its efficiency falls.
labs.law: ηf = Q(0)/Qmax    θ(x)/θ0 = (cosh m(L−x) + β sinh m(L−x))/(cosh mL + β sinh mL)
labs.lawTex: \eta_f = \frac{\dot{Q}(0)}{\dot{Q}_\mathrm{max}} \qquad \frac{\theta(x)}{\theta_0} = \frac{\cosh m(L - x) + \beta \sinh m(L - x)}{\cosh mL + \beta \sinh mL}
labs.lecture: Kugi et al. (2015), section 3.4.3 (pp. 100–101); eq. (3.94); parameters of Aufgabe 3.14 (p. 107)

practice.question: The rod of Aufgabe 3.14: L = 0.5 m, A = 0.01 m², P = 0.5 m, λ = 60 W/(m K), α = αL = 25 W/(m²K), base at 353 K, air at 293 K. What is its fin efficiency ηf?

equations.note: fin equation: conduction along, convection off the sides (derived; the notes solve it in their appendix, not checked)

equations.eq: θ(x)/θ0 = (cosh m(L−x) + β sinh m(L−x))/(cosh mL + β sinh mL)
equations.tex: \frac{\theta(x)}{\theta_0} = \frac{\cosh m(L - x) + \beta \sinh m(L - x)}{\cosh mL + \beta \sinh mL}
equations.note: temperature with a convective tip, θ = T − T∞

equations.eq: Q(0) = λAmθ0 (sinh mL + β cosh mL)/(cosh mL + β sinh mL)
equations.tex: \dot{Q}(0) = \lambda A m \theta_0 \frac{\sinh mL + \beta \cosh mL}{\cosh mL + \beta \sinh mL}

equations.note: fin efficiency (Rippenwirkungsgrad); Qmax with the whole fin at T0

labs.title: Heating a tank of water
labs.idea: Water of uniform temperature heats like a first-order system: it rises towards T∞ + P/(kA) with time constant m0cp/(kA).
labs.law: m0cp dT/dt = P − kA(T − T∞)    T(t) = T∞ + (P/(kA))(1 − e^(−kAt/(m0cp)))
labs.lawTex: m_0 c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}T}{\mathrm{d}t} = P - kA(T - T_\infty) \qquad T(t) = T_\infty + \frac{P}{kA}\Big(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{kA}{m_0 c_p} t}\Big)
labs.lecture: Kugi et al. (2015), section 3.5, Beispiel 3.3 (pp. 101–103); eqs. (3.97)–(3.104)

practice.question: The tank of Beispiel 3.3 holds 1 kg of water (cp = 4190 J/(kg K)) at T∞ = 20 °C; its ceramic wall has A = 0.05 m², L = 5 mm, λ = 1.5 W/(m K), αi = 500 and αa = 10 W/(m²K). What heater power P brings it to the boil (Ts = 100 °C) after ts = 10 min?

equations.eq: m0cp dT/dt = P − kA(T − T∞),  T(0) = T∞
equations.tex: m_0 c_p \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} T(t) = P - kA\big(T(t) - T_\infty\big), \qquad T(0) = T_\infty

equations.note: heat transfer coefficient of the wall

equations.eq: t = ts + (hvm0/(kA(Ts − T∞))) ln(P/(P − kA(Ts − T∞)))
equations.tex: t = t_s + \ln\Big(\frac{P}{P - kA(T_s - T_\infty)}\Big) \frac{h_v m_0}{kA(T_s - T_\infty)}
equations.note: time when all the water has boiled away

labs.title: Finite differences
labs.idea: On a grid, conduction moves each node towards the average of its neighbours; the explicit scheme is stable only for small enough time steps.
labs.law: Ti^(j+1) = Ti^j + (aΔt/Δx²)(Ti−1^j − 2Ti^j + Ti+1^j)    aΔt/Δx² ≤ 1/2
labs.lawTex: T_i^{j+1} = T_i^j + \frac{a\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}\big(T_{i-1}^j - 2T_i^j + T_{i+1}^j\big) \qquad \frac{a\Delta t}{\Delta x^2} \le \frac{1}{2}

practice.question: The steel rod of Aufgabe 3.15 (λ = 60 W/(m K), ρ = 7850 kg/m³, cp = 450 J/(kg K), L = 0.5 m) is cut into N = 10 intervals. What is the largest time step Δt the explicit scheme allows?

equations.tex: \frac{\partial T}{\partial t} = a \frac{\partial^2 T}{\partial x^2}, \quad a = \frac{\lambda}{\rho c_p}, \qquad \frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\Big|_{x=0} = 0, \quad T(t, L) = T_L(t)
equations.note: 1D conduction, no sources; ∂T/∂x = 0 at x = 0, T(t, L) = TL
semi-discrete model, already in state-space form

equations.eq: Ti^(j+1) = Ti^j + (aΔt/Δx²)(Ti−1^j − 2Ti^j + Ti+1^j),  T0^(j+1) = T0^j + (2aΔt/Δx²)(T1^j − T0^j)
equations.tex: T_i^{j+1} = T_i^j + \frac{a\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}\big(T_{i-1}^j - 2T_i^j + T_{i+1}^j\big), \qquad T_0^{j+1} = T_0^j + \frac{2a\Delta t}{\Delta x^2}\big(T_1^j - T_0^j\big)

labs.title: The drive: from model to digital controller
labs.idea: One plant through the whole course: the notes' drive of a DC motor, a twisting shaft and a load. Model it, shape its open loop with a controller, close the loop within the actuator's range, then run the controller on a computer. The steps share one design: change ωC or Φ in step 2 and steps 3 and 4 follow.
labs.lecture: Kugi (2015), chapter 4 (pp. 94–97) and section 5.3 (pp. 131–133); eqs. (4.1)–(4.6), (5.37)–(5.45); the digital step uses (6.89), (6.90) of section 6.6

practice.question: The drive's model (4.3) with the parameters (4.5): what is the static gain of G from the normalised duty cycle uT,n to the load speed ω2?
practice.solution: At rest the shaft carries no torque without load, so iA = 0 and uA = kA·ω: ω2 = uZW·uT,n/kA = 200/0.9 = 222.22 rad/s per unit duty cycle (4.6a).

practice.question: In the design of section 5.3 the targets are ωC = 3 rad/s and Φ = 65°. What gain VR of the compensating controller (5.38) puts the crossover at ωC?
Worked from (5.39), arg L1(3I) = −105.2°. By how much must (1 + sTR)² lower the phase, and so what is TR for Φ = 65° (in seconds)?
practice.solution: The loop needs Φ − 180° = −115°, so (1 + sTR)² must take 9.8°, each factor half: TR = tan(4.9°)/3 = 0.0287 s (5.40). The notes print −104.5° and so 10.5° and TR = 0.0306 s.

equations.note: the converter as an actuator; −1 ≤ uT,n ≤ 1

equations.eq: ẋ = A x + b uA + e ML, x = (iA, ω1, φ1 − φ2, ω2)
equations.note: motor, shaft of stiffness cT and load
from the duty cycle to the load speed
the known terms of L once the pair is cancelled
each of the two lags takes half the phase
the duty cycle the reference asks for
the controller as R(z); not in the notes' example

labs.title: Cooling a voltage regulator
labs.idea: The chapter in one device: a 5 V regulator heats up as it drops its input voltage, and its heat flows through a base plate, a layer of paste and a heat sink to the air. Model it as a thermal RC network, find the highest safe input voltage, watch it warm up, then let the input swing.
labs.law: P = (Ue − Ua)·Ia    Pmax = (TS,max − T∞)/Rges    G(s) = RSB + (RP(1 + sRKCK) + RK)/((1 + sRPCB)(1 + sRKCK) + sRKCB)
labs.lawTex: P = (U_e - U_a) I_a \qquad P_\mathrm{max} = \frac{T_{S,\mathrm{max}} - T_\infty}{R_\mathrm{ges}} \qquad G(s) = R_\mathrm{SB} + \frac{R_P(1 + sR_KC_K) + R_K}{(1 + sR_PC_B)(1 + sR_KC_K) + sR_KC_B}

practice.question: The paste is λ = 0.8 W/(m K) thick H = 30 µm on A = 150 mm². What is its thermal resistance RP?
Without the heat sink (RSB = 5 K/W, RB = 60 K/W, TS,max = 403 K, T∞ = 323 K, Ua = 5 V, Ia = 0.5 A), what is the highest input voltage at steady state?
With the heat sink (RK = 7 K/W) and the paste, what is the highest input voltage at steady state?
The input swings as Ue(t) = 13 V + 7 V·cos(2πft). What is the lowest frequency f that keeps the junction below TS,max with the heat sink?
practice.solution: T̄S = 323 K + 4 W · 12.25 K/W = 372 K (3.131); the swing may add 31 K, so |G(I2πfmin)| = 31 K/3.5 W = 8.86 K/W (3.135). Solved numerically: fmin = 1.429·10⁻³ Hz.

equations.note: a k-value as a thermal resistance
a boundary of the third kind as a resistance
steady state: the capacities carry nothing
the paste as a plane wall; 0.25 K/W

equations.eq: CB = mB cB, CK = mK cK
equations.tex: C_B = m_B c_B, \quad C_K = m_K c_K
P(t) = (\bar{U}_e - U_a) I_a + \hat{U}_e I_a \cos(2\pi f t)
equations.note: the input swinging 6 V to 20 V

equations.eq: G(s) = RSB + (RP(1 + sRKCK) + RK)/((1 + sRPCB)(1 + sRKCK) + sRKCB)
equations.tex: G(s) = R_\mathrm{SB} + \frac{R_P(1 + sR_KC_K) + R_K}{(1 + sR_PC_B)(1 + sR_KC_K) + sR_KC_B}
equations.note: from P to TS, read off Abbildung 3.24b

labs.title: Four controllers on one drive
labs.idea: The same drive, the same reference step, the same load step and the same actuator range, under four controllers from the course: a PI controller, the compensating controller of the worked design, a state controller with a Luenberger observer, and a PI state controller with the same observer. See which is slow, which asks the actuator for too much, which leaves an error under load, and which meets every target.
labs.law: R(s) = VI(1 + sTI)/s    R(s) = VR(1 + 2ξs/ω0 + s²/ω0²)/(s(1 + sTR)²)    u_k = kᵀx̂_k + g r_k    u_k = kxᵀx̂_k + kI xI,k + kP(r_k − y_k)
labs.lawTex: R_\mathrm{PI}(s) = \frac{V_I(1 + sT_I)}{s} \qquad u_k = \mathbf{k}^\mathrm{T}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + g r_k \qquad u_k = \mathbf{k}_x^\mathrm{T}\hat{\mathbf{x}}_k + k_I x_{I,k} + k_P(r_k - y_k)

practice.question: The PI state controller sets kP = 1/(cᵀ(E − Φ)⁻¹Γ) (8.58). For the sampled drive this is one over the plant's static gain V = 222.22 rad/s of (4.6a). What is kP?
practice.solution: cᵀ(E − Φ)⁻¹Γ is the sampled plant's gain at z = 1, which equals G(0) = V = 222.22 for any Ta. So kP = 1/222.22 = 0.0045.

equations.note: the PI controller; R = VI/s when the integrator alone leaves enough phase
